newsitem.title: POLAND: FROZEN POLISH ZLOTY CRAWL TO CURB T-BILL FLOWS.
newsitem.headline: FROZEN POLISH ZLOTY CRAWL TO CURB T-BILL FLOWS.

text.p: The central bank's intention to freeze the zloty crawling peg devaluation factor is seen curbing short-term foreign buying of Polish treasuries as the move would cap interest rate differential, analysts said.

Earlier on Thursday, the National Bank of Poland President Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz told Reuters the zloty crawling peg would not be cut from from the current one percent per month until year-on-year inflation falls to 13 percent.

The government wants to slash year-on-year inflation to 13 percent in December 1997, from 19.5 percent in September and 21.6 percent at the end of 1995, but many analysts said this forecast was too ambitious.
"A steady crawling peg may freeze foreign short-term speculation on Polish treasuries," said Krzysztof Kozuchowski, dealer at ING Bank in Warsaw.

Analysts said the zloty may soften against the basket of currencies in the mid-term as foreign players, who earlier bought Polish treasuries expecting a slow-down in the zloty devaluation in line with offical forecasts, could pull out.
"Foreign investors may start selling bills from their Polish portfolios. This is not a moment for entering the market," said Piotr Korcz, dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.

Analysts said foreign investors, who bought an estimated $1.5 billion of Polish treasuries in early 1996 after the crawling peg was last cut from 1.2 percent per month in early January, have already sold most of their holdings.
The budget plan for 1996 originally assumed the average rate of the monthly zloty devaluation against a basket of five western currencies would be 0.9 percent monthly.
Analysts said that in the longer-term deposits held in western currencies would become relatively more profitable than zloty deposits, prompting banks to increase currency exposure.
"Strong hard currencies amid falling inflation would translate to a natural trend of lengthening currency positions," a chief dealer at a foreign bank here said.
At 1130 GMT, the zloty eased to 1.80/1.75 percent from the centre of its trading band, from 1.87/1.80 percent at 0720 GMT and Wednesday's close.
